courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: The Lorentz force law states that the total electromagnetic force on a point charge is F = qE + q(v cross B) = q(E + v cross B), the two terms being added as vectors and never as numbers, with F in newtons, q in coulombs including its sign, E in N/C (equivalently V/m), v in m/s and B in tesla.

The magnetic term has magnitude F = q*v*B*sin(theta) with theta the angle between v and B, so it vanishes both for a charge at rest and for a charge moving parallel or antiparallel to the field and is greatest when v is perpendicular to B; its direction is given by right-hand rule 1 (thumb along v, fingers along B, force out of the palm) for a positive charge and is reversed for a negative one, and it is always perpendicular to the plane containing v and B.

Because the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant its power F.v is exactly zero, so a magnetic field can bend a charged particle's path but can never change its speed or kinetic energy; only the electric term qE does work, which is why in every accelerator E accelerates and B steers.

In a uniform field a charge with v perpendicular to B moves in a circle of radius r = m*v/(qB) with period T = 2*pi*m/(qB) and cyclotron frequency f = qB/(2*pi*m) that are independent of the speed, while a velocity component along B is untouched and turns the path into a helix of pitch v_parallel*T; crossed electric and magnetic fields transmit undeflected exactly one speed, v = E/B, independent of both charge and mass.

Summing the single-charge law over the moving charges in a conductor, with dq = lambda*dl and I = lambda*v, gives dF = I dl cross B and hence F = I L cross B with magnitude F = B*I*L*sin(theta) for a straight wire in a uniform field, theta being the angle between the current and the field; this is the origin of the torque on a current loop, of the electric motor and of magnetic levitation, and the deck's factors of 1/c belong to Gaussian cgs units and must be dropped in SI.

The week's summary sheet adds electromagnetic oscillations and waves: oscillating electric and magnetic fields sustain one another, are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (which is the direction of E cross B), travel in vacuum at c = 3.00x10^8 m/s so that c = f*lambda, span the spectrum from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays to gamma rays in order of increasing frequency, and carry energy h*f per photon.

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: An improper integral is defined as a limit of proper integrals: (integral from a to infinity of f) = lim as t -> infinity of (integral from a to t of f), and it converges precisely when that limit exists and is finite, so divergence covers both an infinite limit and a limit that fails to exist because of oscillation.

Type I improper integrals have an infinite interval of integration with a continuous integrand, and a doubly infinite integral (from -infinity to infinity) must be split at some interior point c with both halves required to converge separately, which is why the symmetric Cauchy principal value is not an acceptable evaluation.

Type II improper integrals have a finite interval but an integrand with an infinite discontinuity at an endpoint or, more dangerously, at an interior point, where the Fundamental Theorem may not be applied across the singularity and the integral must be split into two one-sided limits.

The two p-tests point in opposite directions: (integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x^p) converges if and only if p > 1 with value 1/(p-1), while (integral from 0 to 1 of dx/x^p) converges if and only if p < 1 with value 1/(1-p), and p = 1 diverges at both ends.

The Comparison Test states that if 0 <= f(x) <= g(x) on [a, infinity) then convergence of (integral of g) forces convergence of (integral of f), and divergence of (integral of f) forces divergence of (integral of g); the other two pairings give no information whatsoever, and the non-negativity hypothesis is what makes the truncated integral increasing and therefore convergent once it is bounded above.

The Limit Comparison Test settles cases where the direct inequality points the wrong way: for positive f and g with lim as x -> infinity of f/g = L and 0 < L < infinity, the two integrals converge or diverge together, the comparison function being obtained by keeping only the dominant terms of numerator and denominator.

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: A simple statement contains only one expression and ends with a semicolon, so more than one statement may sit on a single line and one statement may span several lines; a block, or compound statement, contains more than one statement inside curly brackets, takes no semicolon after its right curly bracket, and is treated by the computer like a single statement, which is exactly what allows it to be used wherever one statement is expected.

Blocks exist so that a complex problem broken into smaller ones can have each solution treated as a single unit, and the course names their three applications as functions, decision making statements (if, if-else, if-else-if) and iterative statements (for, while, do-while).

Booleans represent values that are either true or false, and in C a Boolean variable is declared with the bool keyword; but Boolean values are returned as integers, with 1 or any other number that is not 0 representing true and 0 representing false, so truth in C is the numeric property of being nonzero and an if compares its expression with zero rather than with true.

A Boolean expression is built by comparing values and variables with the relational operators ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= and combining the results with the logical operators &&, || and !; it evaluates to the integer 1 or 0, its operators obey a fixed precedence in which ! binds tighter than relational, relational tighter than equality, equality tighter than &&, && tighter than || and assignment lowest of all, and && and || short-circuit so that the right operand and all of its side effects are skipped once the left operand settles the result.

Programme control is responsible for the sequential execution of a programme from one line to the next until the last line, and branching means the computer can decide to move program control to another line instead: unconditional branching, whose example is goto, moves control without checking any condition, while conditional branching, also called decision making or selection, moves control only if predetermined conditions are satisfied and comprises if, if-else, if-else-if and switch.

Iteration repeats a block: a while loop tests its condition before the body and so may run zero times, a do-while tests after the body and is guaranteed to execute at least one time, and a for loop executes its init step first and only once, then evaluates the condition, then runs the body, then the increment, before testing again - which is why a for control variable holds the first failing value after the loop ends and why i <= n runs one pass more than i < n.

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Specific heat capacity is defined as the heat energy required to raise the temperature of unit mass (1 kg) of a material by one degree Celsius, has the SI unit J/kgK (equivalently J/kg degC), is a property of the material rather than of the sample, and obeys Q = m*c*(T_f - T_i) with Q positive when the body gains heat.

The specific heat of a solid is determined by the method of mixtures: a block of mass m_s heated on a hot plate to T_s (set between 90 and 99 degC) is transferred with crucible tongs into a calorimeter of mass m_c holding water of mass m_w, both initially at room temperature T_r, and the mixture is allowed to reach a single equilibrium temperature T_f.

The working equation is the principle of conservation of energy applied to the mixture, heat lost by the solid equals heat gained by the water and the calorimeter: m_s*c_s*(T_s - T_f) = (m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c)*(T_f - T_r), so c_s = (m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c)*(T_f - T_r) / [m_s*(T_s - T_f)], with c_w = 4186 J/kgK for water and c_c = 387 J/kgK for the copper calorimeter.

The calorimeter term m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c is the total heat capacity of the mixture in J/degC (its water equivalent is that figure divided by c_w); omitting m_c*c_c understates the heat gained and drives the computed specific heat too low, as do heat lost by the block during transfer and heat leaking out of the insulating jacket.

On the deck's own copper data (m_s = 8.9 g, m_c = 36.36 g, m_w = 68.63 g, T_r = 16.1 degC, T_s = 91.3 degC, T_f = 17.0 degC) the heat capacity of water plus calorimeter is 301 J/degC, the heat gained is 271 J and c_s = 410 J/kgK, about 6 percent above copper's accepted 387 J/kgK, the error being dominated by the mere 0.9 degC rise read on a 0.1 degC thermometer.

Repeating the run and plotting the heat gained, (m_w*c_w + m_c*c_c)*(T_f - T_r), against m_s*(T_s - T_f) gives a straight line through the origin whose gradient is the specific heat of the solid c_s in J/kgK, a non-zero intercept signalling heat lost in transfer or through the jacket.

checks.topic: Conceptual session on Week 9 exactly as the deck builds it: the two triggers that make ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx improper; the Type I definitions ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx = lim(t→∞) ∫ₐᵗ f(x)dx and ∫₋∞ᵇ f(x)dx = lim(t→−∞) ∫ₜᵇ f(x)dx, with convergent meaning the limit exists; why ∫₋∞^∞ must be split and why one divergent half ends the question; the three Type II clauses and the one-sided limits c → b⁻ and c → a⁺; the Comparison Test in her lettering 0 ≤ g(x) ≤ f(x), its two valid conclusions and the two that prove nothing; and Note 1, ∫₁^∞ (1/xᵖ)dx converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1.

questions.q: Slide 4 lists exactly two conditions under which the definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx is called improper. Which pair is it?
options: At least one limit of integration is infinite, or the integrand has one or more points of discontinuity on [a, b]
The integrand is discontinuous, or the integrand takes negative values on [a, b]
The interval is infinite, or the antiderivative cannot be written in closed form
The integrand is not differentiable on [a, b], or the interval is unbounded
questions.concept: The two triggers that make an integral improper
questions.why: Her definition has one clause about the limits of integration and one about the integrand: infinite limit (Type I), or a discontinuity somewhere on [a, b] (Type II). Option 2 imports sign, which is irrelevant — plenty of proper integrals are negative. Option 3 confuses a reason to reach for the Comparison Test with the definition; ∫₀^∞ xe⁻ˣdx has a perfectly ordinary antiderivative and is still improper. Option 4 swaps continuity for differentiability; the definition only asks about discontinuity.

questions.q: What does the symbol ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx actually mean, according to slide 5?
options: The area under f from a onwards, computed directly by the Fundamental Theorem
F(∞) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f
lim(t→∞) ∫ₐᵗ f(x)dx, provided that limit exists
The sum of ∫ₐ^b f(x)dx over every b greater than a
questions.concept: The infinite limit is defined by a limit, not evaluated directly
questions.why: She defines it: if ∫ₐᵗ f(x)dx exists for every t ≥ a, then ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx = lim(t→∞) ∫ₐᵗ f(x)dx, provided this limit exists. You replace ∞ by a letter, do an ordinary definite integral, then take the limit — and the first line is worth marks on its own. Option 1 skips the definition and applies the Fundamental Theorem where it does not apply. Option 2 treats ∞ as a number you can substitute into F; it is not one. Option 4 invents an infinite sum, a different object altogether.

questions.q: On slide 5 she says the improper integrals ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx and ∫₋∞ᵇ f(x)dx are called convergent or divergent according to what test?
options: Convergent if the integrand tends to 0, divergent otherwise
Convergent if the corresponding limit exists, divergent if the limit does not exist
Convergent if the region under the curve is bounded, divergent if it is unbounded
Convergent if the integrand is positive throughout, divergent if it changes sign
questions.concept: Convergence is a statement about the limit, nothing else
questions.why: Her wording is exact: convergent if the corresponding limit exists, divergent if it does not. Option 1 names a necessary-looking condition that is not sufficient — 1/x tends to 0 and ∫₁^∞ dx/x still diverges by Note 1 with p = 1. Option 3 is the intuition students carry in and it is wrong in both directions: the region under 1/x² from 1 onwards is unbounded in extent yet the integral converges. Option 4 has nothing to do with it; cos²(x)/x² is positive and convergent, 1/x is positive and divergent.

questions.q: Slide 5 clause 3 says: if ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx and ∫₋∞ᵇ f(x)dx are convergent, then ∫₋∞^∞ f(x)dx = ∫₋∞ᵃ f(x)dx + ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx. What is the role of the words 'are convergent'?
options: They are the conclusion — splitting the integral is what proves each half converges
They are a reminder that the split point must be chosen where f is continuous
They are optional; the sum formula holds for any f
They are a hypothesis — you may only add the two halves once both are known to converge, so a single divergent half makes the whole integral divergent
questions.concept: Both halves must converge before ∫₋∞^∞ is defined
questions.why: Convergence of the halves is what licenses the sum, which is exactly why Type I Example 2 can stop the moment one half runs to ∞ and write 'diverges'. Option 1 reverses hypothesis and conclusion. Option 2 states something true of Type II splitting, not of this clause. Option 3 is the error that produces the illegal cancellation of +∞ against −∞; the definition forbids it precisely by making convergence a hypothesis.

questions.q: Slide 8 clause 1 covers f continuous on [a, b) with an infinite discontinuity at b, and gives ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = lim(c→b⁻) ∫ₐᶜ f(x)dx. Why is the limit one-sided, and from that side?
options: Because the moving endpoint c must stay inside the interval [a, b) where f is continuous, so it can only approach b from below
Because f is only defined for x less than b anywhere on the real line
Because a two-sided limit would give an answer twice as large
Because b⁻ is a notation for the value of b in the previous step of the calculation
questions.concept: Why the Type II limit arrow points into the interval
questions.why: Every ∫ₐᶜ in the limit has to be an ordinary proper integral, so c must sit where f is continuous — inside [a, b). That forces c → b⁻. The mirror clause has the interval (a, b] and the limit c → a⁺: the arrow always points into the interval. Option 2 confuses a local blow-up with a domain restriction; f is usually defined past b, it is just not integrable up to it. Option 3 invents an arithmetic effect limits do not have. Option 4 misreads the minus superscript as bookkeeping rather than as 'from below'.

questions.q: Slide 8 clause 3 deals with f continuous on [a, b] except at some c strictly inside (a, b) where it has an infinite discontinuity. What must you do, and what goes wrong if you do not?
options: Shift the interval to avoid c; otherwise the answer is only approximate
Split as ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫_c^b f and take a one-sided limit into c from each side; otherwise you apply the Fundamental Theorem across a point where the integrand is undefined and can get an impossible answer
Take the limit as c approaches both a and b at once; otherwise you double-count the middle
Nothing special — the single point c has zero width, so it cannot affect a definite integral
questions.concept: An interior discontinuity forces a split before anything else
questions.why: Her clause 3 splits at the bad point and each piece is then a Type II integral of clause 1 or clause 2 type. Type II Example 1 is built on it: ∫₋₁² dx/x⁴ ignores the split and the Fundamental Theorem returns −3/8, a negative number for a strictly positive integrand, which is impossible. Option 1 changes the question. Option 3 misreads which letter is moving. Option 4 is the seductive one — a single point does not matter for a bounded function, but here the function is unbounded near it, and that is the entire difference.

questions.q: Note 1 on slide 11 states the p-test for ∫₁^∞ (1/xᵖ)dx. Where does the boundary case p = 1 fall, and how does Example 2 depend on that?
options: p = 1 converges, and Example 2 uses it to prove ∫₃^∞ dx/√(x² − 1) converges
p = 1 is not covered by Note 1, so Example 2 evaluates ∫₃^∞ dx/x directly instead
p = 1 diverges — Note 1 says converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1 — and Example 2 uses ∫₃^∞ dx/x as the divergent smaller function that drags 1/√(x² − 1) up with it
p = 1 diverges, but Example 2 avoids it by comparing with 1/x² instead
questions.concept: p = 1 sits on the divergent side of Note 1
questions.why: Note 1 is stated as converges if p > 1, diverges if p ≤ 1, so the boundary belongs to divergence — and Example 2 quotes exactly that, calling ∫₃^∞ dx/x divergent 'since p = 1'. Option 1 puts the boundary on the wrong side and would reverse the verdict. Option 2 is what many textbooks do, using a logarithm, but this deck never introduces ln x and simply quotes Note 1. Option 4 invents a different comparison; comparing 1/√(x² − 1) with the convergent 1/x² would in any case be the useless direction.

questions.q: You have continuous functions with 0 ≤ g(x) ≤ f(x) for all x ≥ a, and you have established that ∫ₐ^∞ g(x)dx converges. What does the theorem on slide 10 let you conclude about ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx?
options: That it converges, and to a value at least as large
Nothing at all — this is one of the two directions the theorem does not cover
questions.concept: Knowing the smaller integral converges tells you nothing about the larger
questions.why: Her theorem runs the other way: convergence travels DOWNWARDS from f to g, and divergence travels UPWARDS from g to f. A finite area underneath puts no ceiling on the function above it. One pair settles it: on [1, ∞) take g = 1/x² and f = 1/x, so 0 ≤ g ≤ f, and by Note 1 ∫g converges (p = 2) while ∫f diverges (p = 1) — a convergent smaller one sitting under a divergent bigger one. Option 1 is the false converse of clause 1. Option 2 is equally unfounded; f could just as easily converge, as it does with g = 1/x³ and f = 1/x². Option 3 adds an inequality on values to a conclusion the theorem never reaches, and the value inequality points the wrong way besides.

questions.q: State the Comparison Test exactly as slide 10 states it, hypothesis included, and explain in your own words which of f and g is the larger function in her lettering and how you would remember the two conclusions.
questions.concept: The Comparison Test in the lecturer's own lettering
questions.why: A good answer reproduces the hypothesis first — f and g continuous with 0 ≤ g(x) ≤ f(x) for all x ≥ a — then both clauses: if ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx is convergent then ∫ₐ^∞ g(x)dx is convergent; if ∫ₐ^∞ g(x)dx is divergent then ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx is divergent. It should say clearly that in this deck g is the SMALLER function and f is the LARGER one, which is the reverse of most textbooks, and offer a memory hook such as: the big one convergent drags the small one down with it, the small one divergent drags the big one up with it. It should also note that 0 ≤ g is part of the hypothesis, not decoration — without non-negativity the areas can cancel and the argument collapses.

questions.q: Explain why ∫₋₁² dx/x⁴ is an improper integral at all, given that both its limits of integration are finite numbers, and say what the deck requires you to do about it.
questions.concept: Recognising a Type II integral disguised as an ordinary one
questions.why: A good answer goes back to slide 4: an integral is improper if a limit is infinite OR the integrand has a point of discontinuity on the interval. Here the limits −1 and 2 are finite, so trigger 1 does not apply — but 1/x⁴ is undefined at x = 0, and 0 lies strictly between −1 and 2, so trigger 2 does. That makes it Type II with an INTERIOR discontinuity, so slide 8 clause 3 applies: split as ∫₋₁⁰ + ∫₀², then take lim(c→0⁻) on the left piece and lim(b→0⁺) on the right. The answer should stress that the integral looks completely ordinary on the page and the only way to spot it is to check the zeros of the denominator against the interval before integrating, and can add the consequence of not doing so: the Fundamental Theorem applied straight through returns −3/8, a negative number for a strictly positive integrand.

questions.q: The deck's introduction says: 'Sometimes it is difficult to find the exact value of an improper integral by antidifferentiation. However, it is still possible to determine whether an improper integral converges or diverges.' Explain what the Comparison Test does and does not give you, using her Example 1 on ∫₂^∞ cos²(x)/x² dx.
questions.concept: Comparison decides convergence and never produces a value
questions.why: A good answer separates the verdict from the number. In Example 1 she bounds 0 ≤ cos²(x) ≤ 1, divides by the positive x² to get 0 ≤ cos²(x)/x² ≤ 1/x², sets f = 1/x² and g = cos²(x)/x², evaluates ∫₂^∞ dx/x² = 1/2, and concludes by clause 1 that the original converges. The 1/2 is the value of the COMPARISON integral, not of the original — cos²x has no elementary antiderivative in this combination, which is why comparison was needed. All that follows about the original is that it converges and is at most 1/2. Writing ∫₂^∞ cos²(x)/x² dx = 1/2 is a genuine error. The answer should also note that squaring the cosine is what makes 0 ≤ g hold; with cos x itself the hypothesis fails.

questions.q: Type I Example 1 reaches lim(t→∞)[−te⁻ᵗ − e⁻ᵗ + 1] and the lecturer pauses to apply L'Hôpital's Rule. Explain what needed resolving, how she resolves it, and what the common wrong answer is.
questions.concept: Why −te⁻ᵗ tends to 0 and not to −∞
questions.why: A good answer identifies the problem: as t → ∞ the factor −t tends to −∞ while e⁻ᵗ tends to 0, so −te⁻ᵗ is an indeterminate product. Rewriting e⁻ᵗ as 1/eᵗ turns it into −t/eᵗ, which the slide labels −∞/∞ — a quotient of two quantities both running to infinity, so L'Hôpital's Rule applies. Differentiating numerator and denominator gives −1/eᵗ, and since eᵗ → ∞ this tends to 0. Hence the whole bracket tends to 0 + 0 + 1 = 1 and the integral converges to 1. The common wrong answer is to read −t → −∞ off the front and declare the limit −∞ (hence divergence); the point is that the exponential in the denominator grows faster than any polynomial, so it wins. A good answer may also note that the +1 comes from subtracting the value of −xe⁻ˣ − e⁻ˣ at x = 0, which is −1.

checks.topic: The Lorentz force as concepts: what each term in F = q(E + v cross B) means and the exact conditions under which each one vanishes, why the magnetic force is perpendicular to both v and B and therefore does no work, the RHR-1 direction rule and what reversing the sign of q changes, why the orbit in a uniform field is a circle or a helix and why its period is independent of speed, how the crossed-field velocity selector works, why F = I L cross B is the single-charge law summed over the moving charges in a wire, and the transverse geometry of an electromagnetic wave

questions.q: The magnetic part of the Lorentz force on a charged particle is found to be zero, although the particle is inside a strong uniform magnetic field. The possible reasons are:
options: the field is uniform, and a uniform field exerts no force on a point charge - only a torque on a dipole
the particle is at rest, or its velocity lies along B; in either case v cross B = 0
the particle's charge is negative, so the minus sign cancels the force
the particle's velocity is perpendicular to B, which is where the sine factor passes through zero
questions.concept: The magnetic force needs motion, and motion across the field
questions.why: F = q*v*B*sin(theta) vanishes in exactly two ways: v = 0, so a stationary charge feels nothing magnetic however strong the field; and sin(theta) = 0, that is v parallel or antiparallel to B, since the cross product of parallel vectors is zero - which is why charged particles spiral along field lines rather than across them. (a) misapplies the Week 8 dipole result to a single moving charge, which a uniform field pushes very hard. (c) confuses a sign with a magnitude: a negative charge feels an equal force in the opposite direction, never none. (d) is the sin/cos inversion - v perpendicular to B is where the force is maximum.

questions.q: A charged particle moves through a uniform magnetic field in such a way that the magnetic force on it is a maximum. It follows that:
options: its velocity is parallel to B, the two vectors reinforcing each other
its velocity is perpendicular to B, and the force therefore lies along B
its velocity is perpendicular to B, and the force is perpendicular to both v and B
its velocity is at 45 degrees to B, the angle that balances the sine and cosine factors
questions.concept: Maximum force at theta = 90 degrees, with F still perpendicular to both vectors
questions.why: sin(theta) peaks at 90 degrees, so the force is greatest when v is perpendicular to B, and F = q*v cross B is then perpendicular to the plane containing them - perpendicular to v, hence no work, and perpendicular to B. (a) has the angle exactly backwards; parallel vectors give zero force. (b) is the sharpest distractor: right angle, wrong direction - v cross B is perpendicular to B by construction and can never lie along it. (d) invents a compromise angle by analogy with projectile range; there is no cosine factor in F = q*v*B*sin(theta) to balance.

questions.q: A magnetic field can steer a charged particle but can never increase its kinetic energy. The reason is that:
options: the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so its power F.v is zero at every instant
the magnetic force is far weaker than the electric force at ordinary speeds, so the work it does is negligible
magnetic field lines are closed loops, so any energy gained on one part of the path is given back on another
the magnetic force acts on the particle's spin rather than on its translational motion
questions.concept: F perpendicular to v gives P = F.v = 0 exactly and at every instant
questions.why: Work is the integral of F.dl with dl along v, so a force permanently at right angles to the motion contributes nothing anywhere on the path; speed and kinetic energy are rigorously constant. (b) makes the result a matter of size, which would let a strong enough field do work - it cannot, at any strength. (c) is the most dangerous answer because it nearly argues: it concedes that work is done and claims it cancels round a loop, which would still allow the particle to speed up and slow down within one orbit, and would fail entirely on an unclosed helical path. (d) invents a spin interaction; q*v cross B acts on the translational velocity and the result holds for a spinless particle.

questions.q: A charge enters a uniform magnetic field with velocity components both along and across B, and follows a helix. The helix arises because:
options: the field exerts a force along B that stretches the circular orbit out into a spiral
the component of v along B is never changed, since the force has no component along B, while the perpendicular component is turned in a circle
the field weakens along its own direction, so the radius grows from turn to turn
the particle radiates energy as it circulates, so the closed circle gradually opens out
questions.concept: v cross B has no component along B, so the parallel motion survives untouched
questions.why: F = q*v cross B is perpendicular to B, so it has no component along B: the parallel part of the velocity is never accelerated or retarded and drifts on uniformly, while the perpendicular part feels a constant-magnitude transverse force and is bent into a circle of radius m*v_perp/(qB). Uniform drift plus circle equals helix, of pitch v_parallel * T. (a) asserts a force along B, which the cross product forbids. (c) invents a non-uniform field; in a genuinely converging field the radius would shrink, giving a magnetic mirror. (d) appeals to radiation, negligible here, and the helix appears even in the idealised non-radiating treatment.

questions.q: The period T = 2*pi*m/(qB) of a charged particle's circular orbit does not depend on its speed. This is because:
options: the magnetic force does no work, so no property of the motion can change
the speed cancels because it enters the centripetal expression squared and the magnetic force once
the period is fixed by the field alone, and the field has been specified as uniform
a faster particle sweeps a proportionally larger circle, and the extra path length exactly offsets the extra speed
questions.concept: Circumference and speed are both proportional to v, so they cancel (isochronism)
questions.why: r = m*v_perp/(qB) grows in exact proportion to the speed, so the circumference does too, and T = 2*pi*r/v_perp = 2*pi*m/(qB) has no v in it: a faster particle travels further and proportionately faster, arriving at the same moment - which is what lets a cyclotron run at one fixed frequency. (a) is a true statement used as a non sequitur: no-work fixes the speed of a given particle and says nothing about comparing particles of different speeds. (b) is a pseudo-derivation: q*v*B = m*v^2/r cancels one power of v, leaving r proportional to v, and the second cancellation happens only on dividing the circumference by the speed. (c) is empty - the field is uniform in both cases, and T also depends on m and q.

questions.q: In a velocity selector, one and the same speed passes undeflected for every particle admitted - electrons, protons, heavy ions alike. This is because:
options: both forces are proportional to q, so q cancels, and neither force contains the mass at all
both the electric and the magnetic force are proportional to v, so their ratio is fixed whatever the particle
heavier particles are deflected less, and that compensates exactly for their greater inertia
the field strengths are re-adjusted for each species before its beam is admitted
questions.concept: q cancels from qE = q*v*B and m never appears
questions.why: The balance condition qE = q*v*B divides through by q to give v = E/B - no charge, no sign, no mass; reverse the sign of the charge and both forces reverse together, so the balance survives, which is what makes it a speed filter rather than a species filter. (b) is false about the electric force, which is qE regardless of v - and the whole mechanism depends on that asymmetry, one force depending on speed and the other not, so the two balance at one speed only. (c) invents a mass dependence and then a compensation for it; neither force involves m. (d) describes an apparatus needing constant retuning, which is exactly the labour the selector saves.

questions.q: The force on a current-carrying wire, F = I L cross B, is:
options: an independent law, obtained from Ampere's law rather than from the Lorentz force
a consequence of Newton's third law applied between the field and the wire
valid only for wires, the Lorentz force being valid only for isolated charges, so the two are logically independent
the single-charge law q*v cross B summed over the moving charges: dq = lambda*dl and I = lambda*v give dF = I dl cross B
questions.concept: The wire law is the single-charge law counted per unit length
questions.why: An element dl carrying free charge of linear density lambda drifting at v holds dq = lambda*dl and feels dF = (dq) v cross B = (lambda*dl) v cross B; since I = lambda*v this is dF = I dl cross B, integrating to F = I L cross B with magnitude B*I*L*sin(theta). It is the same physics counted per unit length instead of per particle. (a) confuses the two halves of magnetostatics: Ampere's law says what a current produces, the Lorentz force says what a field does to a current. (b) misuses Newton's third law, which relates forces between two currents and cannot by itself yield B*I*L*sin(theta). (c) makes two laws where there is one and leaves no account of why the constants agree.

questions.q: The deck writes the force on a current element as dF = (I/c) dl cross B. Judged as an SI formula, this expression:
options: is correct, the c being the conversion from amperes to the units in which B is measured
is correct only for relativistic currents, in which the drift speed approaches c
is the cgs (Gaussian) form; in SI the factor 1/c is absent and the law reads dF = I dl cross B
is dimensionally sound in both systems, so either version may be used with SI data
questions.concept: The factor 1/c belongs to Gaussian cgs units, not to SI
questions.why: In Gaussian units the magnetic force is written q(v/c) cross B and the current-element force (I/c) dl cross B, because B is defined so that E and B share dimensions; in SI there is no c, and F = q*v cross B, dF = I dl cross B. Dividing an SI answer by 3x10^8 makes it wrong by that factor. (a) invents a unit conversion for a current measured in amperes on both sides. (b) confuses the drift speed of the charges - under a millimetre per second in copper - with the constant c, which the cgs formula carries whatever the drift speed. (d) is the costliest answer: the two forms are not dimensionally interchangeable, and mixing systems produces answers wrong by eight orders of magnitude.

questions.q: Explain why the magnetic force does no work, and say exactly what is conserved as a result and what is not. Then explain why 'does no work' is not the same as 'exerts no force' and not the same as 'produces no acceleration'. Finish by explaining how a cyclotron nevertheless raises a proton's energy to many MeV.
questions.concept: The no-work property of the magnetic force, and what it does and does not forbid
questions.why: The magnetic force F = q*v cross B is perpendicular to both its factors, in particular perpendicular to v at every instant; work is the integral of F.dl with dl along v, so the integrand is identically zero and the instantaneous power P = F.v = 0. Hence the speed and the kinetic energy are exactly conserved however strong the field and however long the particle stays in it. What is not conserved is the momentum p = m*v, a vector whose direction turns continuously and reverses completely over half a revolution; nor is the velocity. 'Does no work' is not 'exerts no force': there is a real force of magnitude q*v*B, large enough to bend a proton beam round a 27 km ring. It is also not 'produces no acceleration': a = q*v*B/m is real and is what curves the path - a centripetal acceleration that changes the direction of v and not its magnitude, and confusing acceleration with speeding up is the error this topic exposes. A cyclotron therefore never uses the magnetic field to add energy. The field's job is to bend the protons round semicircles inside the dees and, because T = 2*pi*m/(qB) is independent of speed, to return them to the gap at strictly regular intervals. The energy comes entirely from the electric field across that gap: each crossing finds the alternating voltage reversed so that qE accelerates the proton again, adding qV of kinetic energy, and the radius grows as r = m*v/(qB) until after hundreds of crossings the proton spirals out at many MeV. Every joule came from E and none from B.

questions.q: From the two defining properties of the cross product, explain why the magnetic force is zero when v is parallel to B and greatest when v is perpendicular to B, and why the force is perpendicular to both. Then explain what reversing the sign of the charge does, and reconcile these two facts: an electron and a proton fired in the same direction through the same field curve opposite ways, yet an electron beam and a positive-ion beam travelling in opposite directions curve the same way.
questions.concept: The geometry of v cross B and the effect of the sign of q
questions.why: A cross product has two defining properties. Magnitude |v cross B| = v*B*sin(theta), theta being the angle between the vectors: zero when they are parallel or antiparallel (sin(theta) = 0) and greatest when they are perpendicular (sin(theta) = 1). Direction: v cross B is perpendicular to the plane containing v and B, with the sense given by the right hand. Both facts about the magnetic force follow at once - a charge moving along a field line feels nothing and travels straight, a charge moving across the field feels the full q*v*B, and the force is perpendicular to v, which is why it does no work, and perpendicular to B, which is why motion along B is never affected. RHR-1 as the deck states it - thumb along v, fingers along B, force out of the palm - expresses that sense and gives the force on a positive charge. Reversing the sign of q reverses F, because q multiplies the whole vector; for an electron, compute the positive-charge answer and turn it round. The two observations are reconciled by noticing that F depends on the product q*v, not on q or v separately. An electron and a proton fired the same way have opposite q and the same v, so q*v is opposite and the forces are opposite: they curve apart. An electron beam moving one way and a positive-ion beam moving the other have opposite q and opposite v, and the two reversals cancel, so q*v is the same and they curve the same way - which is exactly why a conventional current to the right and an electron flow to the left are the same current and feel the same force.

questions.q: Explain the mechanism of the crossed-field velocity selector: why exactly one speed passes undeflected, why that speed is E/B and contains neither the charge nor the mass, what happens to particles faster and slower than the selected speed and which force wins in each case, and how adding a second, magnet-only stage converts the apparatus into a mass spectrometer.
questions.concept: The velocity selector: one speed-dependent force set against one speed-independent force
questions.why: Arrange E and B perpendicular to each other and both perpendicular to the beam. A particle of charge q and speed v then feels an electric force qE, whose size does not depend on v, and a magnetic force q*v*B, whose size is proportional to v, with the geometry set so that the two oppose. Undeflected passage requires qE = q*v*B, hence v = E/B. Two features carry the physics. First, q cancels, sign included: reversing the charge reverses both forces together, so electrons and positive ions of the same speed both pass. Second, m never appears, since neither force involves the mass. The selected speed is a property of the apparatus, not of the particle. Because one force grows with v and the other does not, the balance holds at exactly one speed: a particle faster than E/B has q*v*B > qE, so the magnetic force wins and deflects it to the side the magnetic force points; a slower particle has q*v*B < qE, so the electric force wins and deflects it the other way. Both miss the exit slit. Passing the surviving beam into a second region containing B alone bends it into a circle of radius r = m*v/(q*B'), and since v is now known and fixed by the first stage, the radius measures m/q directly: heavier ions of the same charge sweep proportionally larger circles. The division of labour is the point - the first stage removes the speed spread that would blur the mass measurement, and the second separates by mass.

questions.q: For a plane electromagnetic wave, explain why E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, and what sustains the wave as it travels. Explain why the frequency and the wavelength are inversely related while the speed is fixed at c, and state what physically distinguishes a gamma ray from a radio wave given that both travel at exactly the same speed.
questions.concept: The transverse geometry of an electromagnetic wave, and c = f*lambda
questions.why: An electromagnetic wave is a self-sustaining pair of oscillating fields: a changing electric field generates a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field generates an electric field, so once launched - for instance by the oscillating current in a transmitting aerial - the disturbance regenerates itself and travels away. The generation is by a cross-product relation, so each field is produced at right angles to the one producing it: hence E perpendicular to B, and both perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is the direction of E cross B. The wave is therefore transverse, with no component of either field along the direction of propagation; the standard wrong picture, with E oscillating back and forth along the line of travel, describes a longitudinal wave such as sound and cannot be electromagnetic at all. The speed in vacuum is fixed by the electric and magnetic properties of free space, c = 3.00x10^8 m/s, and is the same for every electromagnetic wave whatever its frequency. Since the wave advances one wavelength per period, c = f*lambda, and because c is constant, f and lambda are inversely proportional. The only physical difference between a gamma ray and a radio wave is that frequency and what follows from it: both are the same transverse E-B disturbance at the same speed, but the gamma ray has an enormously higher frequency, a correspondingly shorter wavelength, and therefore an enormously larger energy per photon, E = h*f = h*c/lambda - a few MeV against a fraction of a microelectronvolt. That is why gamma rays ionise and radio waves do not, and why radio waves diffract round buildings while gamma rays travel in essentially straight lines.

checks.topic: Boolean expressions, statements and control flow as concepts, exactly as the two decks give them: what makes a value true in C and what a comparison returns, the definitions of a simple statement and of a block and why a block counts as a single statement, why blocks exist and where they are used, programme control and branching with unconditional versus conditional, the deck's count of the decision making statements and the switch it teaches outside that count, and the entry condition of if, if-else, if-else-if, switch, while, do-while and for.

questions.q: In C, which one of these conditions is FALSE?
questions.concept: Truth in C is 'not zero'; falsity is 'exactly zero'
questions.why: The deck's rule is that 'Boolean values are returned as integers with; 1 (or any other number that is not 0) represents true, 0 represents false.' Each condition is an expression, so it is worked out first and then tested against zero: 6 - 6 is 0, and 0 is the one value that is false. Option (A) is -3, which is not 0 and is therefore TRUE - the parenthesis in the deck's sentence says 'any other number that is not 0' and says nothing about sign, and a negative value catches out more students than any other. Option (B) is 5 and option (C) is 7, both plainly non-zero. The commonest wrong reading is that a condition must equal 1 to be true, which would make all three of the distractors false as well.

questions.q: The deck says a block is 'treated like a single statement by the computer'. Which consequence follows DIRECTLY from that sentence?
options: That the statements inside a block are executed as one indivisible step, so that no other part of the programme is able to interrupt them part-way through
That the compiler compresses the block into one machine instruction, which is why a block runs faster than the same statements written separately
That a block may be written anywhere a single statement is allowed, which is what lets an if or a while control several statements at once
That the statements inside a block share one semicolon, which is why the closing curly bracket does not need one of its own
questions.concept: The 'one statement' property is a syntactic fact, and it is what makes braces load-bearing
questions.why: 'Treated like a single statement' is a statement about where a block may be written, not about how fast it runs or how it is interrupted. Each of if, while and for governs exactly ONE statement; a block is the device that turns several statements into one, which is why the deck lists functions, decision making statements and iterative statements as the places blocks are used. Option (A) reads it as an atomicity guarantee, which the deck never claims. Option (B) invents a speed claim. Option (D) gets the brace rule right by accident and the reason for it wrong - the closing bracket takes no semicolon because it closes the construct, not because the statements inside are sharing one.

questions.q: Which is the deck's definition of a SIMPLE statement?
options: It contains only one expression and it ends with a semicolon
It contains only one expression and it ends at the end of the line it is written on
It contains any number of expressions and it ends with a semicolon
It is any line of code that does not contain curly brackets
questions.concept: A simple statement: one expression, terminated by a semicolon
questions.why: 'A simple statement contains only one expression and it ends with a semicolon.' Both halves matter, and the second is the one with consequences: the semicolon is the terminator, not the line ending, which is why the deck can ask 'Can we have more than one statement on a single line?' and why one statement may be spread over several lines. Option (B) makes the layout do the work, which is true in some other languages and false in C. Option (C) drops the 'only one expression' half. Option (D) defines a statement by what it lacks, and would make the header of an if into a statement.

questions.q: Why does the deck say we need blocks?
options: Because a programme runs faster when its statements are grouped inside curly brackets
Because while breaking complex problems into smaller ones we need to treat solutions to the smaller problems as single units
Because the compiler needs the curly brackets in order to know where each of the statements inside the block ends and the next one begins
Because a Boolean expression may only be tested inside curly brackets
questions.concept: Blocks exist for problem decomposition, not for tidiness
questions.why: The deck gives the reason twice, and it is about problem solving rather than syntax: 'We need blocks because while trying to solve complex problems by breaking them into smaller ones, we need to treat solutions to the smaller problems as single units', and 'the group of statements inside a block are treated like a single statement by the computer, which essentially means that solutions from different blocks can be seen as solutions to the smaller problems.' Option (C) gives the semicolon's job to the curly brackets - the semicolon ends a statement, the brackets group several. Option (A) invents a speed argument. Option (D) invents a rule about Booleans; a condition is tested wherever it is written.

questions.q: The deck names the places where blocks are used. Which list is it?
options: Decision making statements and iterative statements only
Every statement in C, since each one is a block containing a single statement
Functions, decision making statements, and iterative statements
questions.concept: Where blocks are used, and the deck's examples of each kind
questions.why: 'We use blocks when writing functions, decision making statements, and iterative statements.' The deck then names the members of the last two groups: the decision making statements are the 'if', 'if-else' and 'else-if' statements, and the iterative statements are the 'for', 'while' and 'do-while' statements. Options (A) and (B) each drop part of the deck's list. Option (C) inverts the relationship: a block is made out of statements, and a single statement is not a block - which is exactly why an if without curly brackets governs one statement and no more.

questions.q: A loop's condition is already false at the moment control first reaches the loop. Which statement is correct?
options: A while runs its body once and a do-while runs it zero times, since do-while checks the condition before committing to a pass
Both run their bodies zero times, since a condition that is false at the outset means there is nothing at all for either of the two constructs to do
A while runs its body zero times and a do-while runs it once, since a do-while tests the condition after the body and so runs at least one time
Both run their bodies once, since a loop must always complete one pass before it has anything to test
questions.concept: while tests before the body, do-while after; only do-while is guaranteed to run at least once
questions.why: The while slide says the loop 'iterates while the condition is true' and that 'when the condition becomes false, the program control passes to the line immediately following the loop' - the test comes first, so a condition already false means no pass at all. The do-while slide says it 'works the same way as a while loop, except the fact that it is guaranteed to execute at least one time'. Option (A) has the two rules the right way round in the sentence and the wrong way round on the constructs, which is the classic swap. Option (B) applies the while rule to both and throws away the deck's one distinguishing sentence. Option (D) applies the do-while rule to both, which would make a zero-pass loop impossible.

questions.q: A programmer replaces  if (n > 100) A; else if (n > 50) B; else C;  with three separate if statements carrying the same three conditions. What has changed?
options: Nothing at all, provided the three conditions have been copied out exactly, since the same tests are being applied to the same value in both versions
In the chain the first true condition wins, so at most one branch runs; with three separate ifs each condition is tested independently, so n = 200 runs A and B and C
The chain is faster because it stops testing early, but the three separate ifs produce identical output, so the change is only a matter of efficiency
The three separate ifs can no longer run C, because a bare else is the only construct that can execute when no condition is satisfied
questions.concept: An if-else-if chain stops at the first true condition; separate ifs test every condition independently
questions.why: The deck's if-else-if slide says that with it 'more that two choices are integrated into the decision making process', and the if-else slide says control moves into the if block when the condition is satisfied and 'otherwise' to the else - the word otherwise is what chains the branches together. Broken into separate ifs, each condition is a fresh decision: with n = 200, n > 100 is true, n > 50 is also true, and the final else has become an else on the third if alone. Option (C) sees the early stopping and misses that it changes WHICH code runs. Option (D) invents a limitation on else. Option (A) is the assumption the question exists to break.

questions.q: Which pair of statements matches the deck's definitions of unconditional and conditional branching?
options: Unconditional branching moves control to a statement or block without checking any condition, goto being the example; conditional branching moves it only if predetermined conditions are satisfied
Unconditional branching is the normal sequential movement from one line to the next, and conditional branching is any statement that interrupts it

Unconditional branching is performed by the loops, because a loop repeats regardless of what any single statement in it says, whereas conditional branching is performed by if, because only if mentions a condition at all
Unconditional branching is decided by the compiler before the programme runs, whereas conditional branching is decided while it runs, which is why goto costs nothing at run time
questions.concept: The deck's definitions of unconditional and conditional branching
questions.why: Word for word: 'With unconditional branching, some unconditional statements can move program control to either a specific statement or block without checking any condition', the example being goto, of which the deck says 'the goto statement did not specify any condition before moving program control'. And: 'With conditional branching, the normal flow of operation in our code is also altered but where program control moves to is dependent on if some predetermined conditions are satisfied or not. Conditional branching statements are also known as decision making or selection statements.' Option (B) redefines ordinary sequential flow as branching, when the deck's point is that branching is the DEPARTURE from 'the usual movement from one line to the next line'. Option (C) mislabels loops. Option (D) invents a compile-time/run-time split; goto branches while the programme runs.

questions.q: Explain what a Boolean is in the deck's terms, how a Boolean variable is declared in C and what values it may take, and state precisely what the deck says Boolean values are RETURNED as. Then explain what the deck means by "comparing values and variables" and what such a comparison returns. Finally, use the deck's rule to say which of these conditions are true and which false, and why: if (7), if (0), if (-2), if (3 - 3).
questions.concept: A Boolean, a Boolean variable, and the integer rule that decides every condition
questions.why: WHAT A BOOLEAN IS: 'Booleans represent values that are either true or false.' HOW ONE IS DECLARED: 'In C programming language, a Boolean variable is declared with the bool keyword and it can only take the values true or false.' WHAT THEY ARE RETURNED AS - the examinable sentence: 'It is noteworthy that Boolean values are returned as integers with; 1 (or any other number that is not 0) represents true, 0 represents false.' So truth in C is a NUMERIC property. The test a condition undergoes is not a comparison with true; it is a comparison with zero, and everything that is not zero passes it. COMPARING VALUES AND VARIABLES: 'To make decisions and find answers in programming, it is sometimes useful to compare values and variables. When this comparison activity takes place, the return value is usually a Boolean value.' Two things follow. First, a comparison is not a question the machine asks; it is an expression that HAS a value, exactly as 3 + 4 has the value 7. Second, by the previous rule that value arrives as an integer, 1 or 0, which is why a comparison can be printed, stored or used anywhere a number can. THE FOUR CONDITIONS: if (7) is TRUE, because 7 is not 0. if (0) is FALSE, because 0 is the value the rule names as false. if (-2) is TRUE, because the rule says 'any other number that is not 0', and it says nothing about sign - a negative value is just as true as a positive one, which is the part students most often get wrong. if (3 - 3) is FALSE, because the expression is evaluated first and its value is 0. In every case the machine does the same single thing: work out the value, and ask whether it is zero.

questions.q: Define programme control as the deck defines it, and say why a programmer would ever want to alter it. Then define branching, distinguish unconditional from conditional branching, give the deck's example of an unconditional statement and say what the deck observes about it, and give the two other names the deck offers for conditional branching statements. End by naming the three decision making statements the deck lists.
questions.concept: Programme control, branching, and the two kinds of branch
questions.why: PROGRAMME CONTROL: 'In the C programming language, programme control is responsible for the sequential execution of a programme from one line to the next line until it reached the last line of the programme.' That is the default behaviour of a programme - straight down the page. WHY ALTER IT: 'For some problem solving application, we want to alter this flow of operation to ensure that programme control moves to either a specific statement or block in our code.' Real problems need decisions and repetition, and neither is possible if control can only fall from one line to the next. BRANCHING: 'Branching basically means that the computer can decide to move program control to another line of code instead of the usual movement from one line to the next line.' UNCONDITIONAL: 'With unconditional branching, some unconditional statements can move program control to either a specific statement or block without checking any condition.' The deck's example is the goto statement, and its observation about it is that 'the goto statement did not specify any condition before moving program control' - the jump happens every time control reaches it, with nothing tested. CONDITIONAL: 'With conditional branching, the normal flow of operation in our code is also altered but where program control moves to is dependent on if some predetermined conditions are satisfied or not.' THE TWO OTHER NAMES: conditional branching statements 'are also known as decision making or selection statements'. THE THREE DECISION MAKING STATEMENTS: 'There are three types of decision making statements. The three statements are the "if", "if-else" and "if-else-if" statements.' The deck adds that 'each of these statements are usually blocks consisting of one or more statements', which is where the week's two halves join: branching decides which block runs, and a block is what makes several statements into one.

questions.q: The deck states, on its Conditional branching slide and again on its SUMMARY slide, that there are three types of decision making statement, and it names them. It then teaches a fourth statement under the same heading. Name the three, name the fourth, give the deck's one-sentence description of the fourth, and explain how a student who memorised the summary and a student who worked through the slides can give different answers to "how many decision making statements are there?" - both of them reading the deck correctly. Say what you would write in an examination.
questions.concept: The deck's count of the decision making statements disagrees with the deck's own slides
questions.why: THE THREE: 'There are three types of decision making statements. The three statements are the "if", "if-else" and "if-else-if" statements.' The SUMMARY slide repeats the same three word for word. THE FOURTH: switch, taught on the slides headed 'Conditional branching: switch', immediately after the if-else-if slides and under the same heading. THE DECK'S DESCRIPTION OF IT: 'With the switch statement, we can execute one code block among many alternatives.' That single sentence is the whole of what the deck says about switch, and it is what an examination can fairly ask. HOW THE TWO STUDENTS DIVERGE. The one who learned the SUMMARY answers 'three - if, if-else and if-else-if', because that is what the deck states twice and states as a count. The one who worked through the slides answers 'four kinds of conditional branching, switch among them', because switch is presented as a conditional branching statement, in the conditional branching sequence, doing exactly what the definition of conditional branching describes - moving control depending on whether a predetermined condition is satisfied. Neither student has misread anything. The deck disagrees with itself: it states a total of three and then teaches a fourth member of the same family. WHAT TO WRITE IN AN EXAMINATION. Answer the count when the question quotes the count - 'the lecture states that there are three: if, if-else and if-else-if' - and then add the sentence that closes the gap: 'the lecture also teaches switch under Conditional branching, describing it as executing one code block among many alternatives, although its stated total of three does not include it.' That answers what was asked and shows that the inconsistency was noticed rather than missed, which is the safest thing to do with an error in the material.

questions.q: For each of if, if-else, if-else-if, switch, while, do-while and for, give the deck's own description and say exactly when the body is entered. For for, say which of its three parts runs only once and what happens next. Then explain why if-else and two separate if statements are not interchangeable, and why a while whose condition is false at the outset behaves differently from a do-while with the same condition.
questions.concept: The entry condition of every control construct in the week
questions.why: IF: 'With the if statement, program control will only move inside the if block if some conditions are satisfied, or else, the entire block will be skipped.' Entered once when the condition is satisfied, not at all otherwise. IF-ELSE: 'With the if-else statement, if some conditions are satisfied, program control will move inside the if block, otherwise, it will move to the else statement block.' One of the two blocks is always entered, and never both. IF-ELSE-IF: 'With the if-else-if statement, more that two choices are integrated into the decision making process.' Control enters the branch whose condition is satisfied. SWITCH: 'With the switch statement, we can execute one code block among many alternatives.' Control enters the block belonging to the alternative that matches. WHILE: 'The loop iterates while the condition is true. When the condition becomes false, the program control passes to the line immediately following the loop.' The condition is tested BEFORE the body, so the body may be entered zero times; the deck adds that 'the condition may be any expression, and true is any nonzero value'. DO-WHILE: it 'works the same way as a while loop, except the fact that it is guaranteed to execute at least one time' - the body is entered before the condition is consulted at all. FOR: 'The init step is executed first, and only once. Next, the condition is evaluated. If it is true, the body of the loop is executed. If it is false, the body of the loop does not execute.' So the INIT step is the part that runs only once; after it, the condition decides, and the body may be entered zero times. WHY IF-ELSE IS NOT TWO IFS: with if-else exactly one branch runs, because the else is reached precisely when the if was not - that is what 'otherwise' means. Two separate ifs are two independent decisions, so both bodies can run, and a second condition that was written assuming the first had failed will now fire when it should not. WHY WHILE AND DO-WHILE DIVERGE: the difference is only where the test sits. With a condition false at the outset, the while tests first, finds it false and passes control to the line immediately following the loop, so nothing in the body happens; the do-while runs the body once and only then tests, so the body has already happened by the time the condition is found to be false. Every other feature of the two is the same, which is why the deck defines the second entirely by its exception to the first.

checks.topic: Problems-only session on Week 9. Evaluate Type I integrals by writing ∫ₐ^∞ f(x)dx = lim(t→∞) ∫ₐᵗ f(x)dx and finishing the limit, including the L'Hôpital step on −te⁻ᵗ; split ∫₋∞^∞ and stop at the first divergent half; split ∫₋₁² dx/x⁴ at the interior discontinuity and get the signs right; and run her four-step comparison template — drop the additive term, take the root, flip on reciprocals, read off p — on ∫₁^∞ dx/√(x⁵ + 3), ∫₂^∞ cos²(x)/x^(3/2) dx, ∫₃^∞ dx/√(x⁴ + 9) and the TASK, ∫₁^∞ dx/√(x⁶ + 1), quoting Note 1 each time.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀^∞ xe⁻ˣ dx.
questions.concept: Type I evaluation with a by-parts antiderivative and L'Hôpital
questions.why: Write it as lim(t→∞) ∫₀ᵗ xe⁻ˣdx = lim(t→∞)[−xe⁻ˣ − e⁻ˣ]|₀ᵗ = lim(t→∞)(−te⁻ᵗ − e⁻ᵗ + 1). The middle term e⁻ᵗ → 0, and −te⁻ᵗ = −t/eᵗ is −∞/∞, so L'Hôpital gives −1/eᵗ → 0. Total: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1. Option 2 loses the +1, which comes from subtracting the value −1 that the antiderivative takes at x = 0. Option 3 keeps that −1 without flipping its sign under the subtraction. Option 4 is what you get from claiming −te⁻ᵗ → −∞; the exponential beats the linear factor.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₃^∞ dx/x².
questions.concept: Finishing a p-integral as a limit rather than quoting Note 1
questions.why: lim(t→∞)[−1/x]|₃ᵗ = lim(t→∞)(−1/t + 1/3) = 1/3, since −1/t → 0. Note 1 only tells you it converges; the limit tells you to what. Option 1 substitutes 3 into the integrand 1/x² instead of into the antiderivative −1/x. Option 3 inverts the answer. Option 4 confuses p = 2 with the divergent side of Note 1; p = 2 > 1 converges.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₁^∞ dx/x^(3/2).
questions.concept: A convergent p-integral with a fractional exponent, evaluated in full
questions.why: The antiderivative of x^(−3/2) is x^(−1/2)/(−1/2) = −2/√x, so lim(t→∞)[−2/√x]|₁ᵗ = lim(t→∞)(−2/√t + 2) = 2. Option 1 misapplies Note 1: p = 3/2 > 1, the convergent side. Option 2 is 1/p, guessed rather than derived. Option 4 comes from dividing by the new power 3/2 without the sign, i.e. treating the exponent as +3/2 instead of −3/2.

questions.q: By Note 1, which of these diverges?
questions.concept: Reading p off a fractional exponent and testing it against 1
questions.why: Note 1: ∫₁^∞ (1/xᵖ)dx converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1. Here p = 2/3, and 2/3 < 1, so it diverges. Options 1 and 2 have p = 5/2 and p = 2, both comfortably above 1. Option 3 is the one that catches people out — 1.01 is barely above 1, but Note 1 draws a hard line and 1.01 > 1, so it converges. Only the exponent's position relative to 1 matters, never how close it is.

questions.q: The TASK slide: determine whether ∫₁^∞ dx/√(x⁶ + 1) converges or diverges.
options: Diverges: comparison with 1/x, which has p = 1
questions.concept: The lecturer's comparison template applied to her own TASK
questions.why: For x ≥ 1, x⁶ + 1 ≥ x⁶, so √(x⁶ + 1) ≥ √(x⁶) = x³, and taking reciprocals of positives reverses it: 1/√(x⁶ + 1) ≤ 1/x³. With f = 1/x³ (convergent, p = 3 > 1 by Note 1) and g the given integrand, clause 1 gives convergence. Option 2 fails to flip the inequality at the reciprocal step, which is the single most common error in this topic. Option 3 forgets to take the square root, so the exponent is not halved. Option 4 compares with the wrong power and then draws divergence from an inequality that would in any case be the useless direction.

questions.q: Determine whether ∫₋₁² dx/x⁴ converges or diverges, and give its value if it has one.
questions.concept: Interior discontinuity: split first, and both pieces run to +∞
questions.why: 1/x⁴ is undefined at x = 0, inside [−1, 2], so slide 8 clause 3 forces the split. With F(x) = −1/(3x³): the left piece is lim(c→0⁻)(−1/(3c³) − 1/3) = +∞, since c³ → 0 from below; the right piece is lim(b→0⁺)(−1/24 + 1/(3b³)) = +∞. Neither limit is finite, so the integral diverges. Option 1 is exactly what the Fundamental Theorem returns if you drive straight through x = 0 — and its negativity, for a strictly positive integrand, is the tell that something is wrong. Option 2 is that same slip with the limits reversed. Option 4 is the upper-limit term alone.

questions.q: Determine whether ∫₁^∞ dx/√(x⁵ + 3) converges or diverges.
options: Diverges, by comparison with 1/x, which has p = 1
No conclusion is available, because the inequality points the wrong way
questions.concept: Halving the exponent when the root is taken
questions.why: For x ≥ 1, x⁵ + 3 ≥ x⁵, so √(x⁵ + 3) ≥ √(x⁵) = x^(5/2), hence 1/√(x⁵ + 3) ≤ 1/x^(5/2). Note 1 with p = 5/2 > 1 gives convergence of the comparison integral, and clause 1 carries it back. Option 1 compares with a function that is far too large and in the useless direction besides. Option 3 skips the square root, leaving p = 5 — the verdict survives by luck, but the comparison function is wrong and the inequality as stated is false. Option 4 misreads the direction: dropping the +3 makes the denominator smaller and hence the fraction bigger, so the given integrand really is the smaller one, which is exactly the case clause 1 handles.

questions.q: A student writes: on [2, ∞), 1/√(x² + 1) ≤ 1/x; ∫₂^∞ dx/x diverges by Note 1 since p = 1; therefore ∫₂^∞ dx/√(x² + 1) diverges. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — both the inequality and the conclusion follow correctly
The inequality is backwards; in fact 1/√(x² + 1) ≥ 1/x
Note 1 is stated for ∫₁^∞ and cannot be used with a lower limit of 2
The reasoning is invalid: the given function is the smaller one, and a divergent larger function licenses no conclusion about what sits underneath it
questions.concept: A correct inequality pointing in the useless direction
questions.why: The inequality is right — x² + 1 > x² gives √(x² + 1) > x and so 1/√(x² + 1) < 1/x — but it makes the given integrand g, the smaller function, and 1/x the larger f. The theorem offers only 'f convergent ⟹ g convergent' and 'g divergent ⟹ f divergent'; 'f divergent ⟹ ?' is one of the two boxes that carry no information, as 1/x² sitting under the divergent 1/x shows. Option 1 accepts an invalid proof of a verdict that happens to be true — a real trap, because being right by accident earns nothing. Option 2 misstates a correct inequality. Option 3 is a red herring: the finite piece ∫₁² dx/x is an ordinary number and cannot change a tail's fate, which is why Example 2 applies Note 1 at lower limit 3.

questions.q: Work Type I Example 1 in full: determine whether ∫₀^∞ xe⁻ˣ dx converges or diverges. Show the limit line, verify the antiderivative by differentiating it, and show the L'Hôpital step explicitly.
questions.concept: A complete Type I evaluation, antiderivative check included
questions.why: A good answer opens with the definition line: ∫₀^∞ xe⁻ˣdx = lim(t→∞) ∫₀ᵗ xe⁻ˣdx. It names the antiderivative −xe⁻ˣ − e⁻ˣ (from parts with u = x and dv = e⁻ˣdx, giving v = −e⁻ˣ and ∫xe⁻ˣdx = −xe⁻ˣ + ∫e⁻ˣdx = −xe⁻ˣ − e⁻ˣ) and checks it: the derivative of −xe⁻ˣ − e⁻ˣ is −e⁻ˣ + xe⁻ˣ + e⁻ˣ = xe⁻ˣ, the integrand. It then evaluates: [−xe⁻ˣ − e⁻ˣ]|₀ᵗ = (−te⁻ᵗ − e⁻ᵗ) − (0 − 1) = −te⁻ᵗ − e⁻ᵗ + 1, spelling out that the lower limit contributes +1. It resolves the indeterminate term by rewriting −te⁻ᵗ as −t/eᵗ, identifying the form −∞/∞, applying L'Hôpital to get −1/eᵗ, and noting that eᵗ → ∞ so the limit is 0. It concludes the whole limit is 0 + 0 + 1 = 1, so the integral converges to 1. Credit the explicit statement that this is a convergent integral WITH a value — unlike anything decided by comparison.

questions.q: Work Type I Example 2 in full: determine whether ∫₋∞^∞ (2x² − x + 3)dx converges or diverges. Show the split, the two independent limits, the antiderivative, and say at what point in the working you are entitled to stop.
questions.concept: Splitting a doubly-infinite integral and stopping at the first divergent half
questions.why: A good answer splits at 0 as she does: ∫₋∞^∞(2x² − x + 3)dx = ∫₋∞⁰(2x² − x + 3)dx + ∫₀^∞(2x² − x + 3)dx, then writes the two halves with DIFFERENT moving letters, lim(a→−∞)∫ₐ⁰ and lim(b→∞)∫₀ᵇ, noting that they are independent and may not be tied into one symmetric limit. The antiderivative is the term-by-term power rule, 2x³/3 − x²/2 + 3x. Evaluating the right half gives 2b³/3 − b²/2 + 3b − 0, which is dominated by 2b³/3 and runs to +∞. That is the stopping point: clause 3 of slide 5 permits the two halves to be added only IF both converge, so a single divergent half settles the question and the integral diverges. A strong answer adds that the left half also runs to +∞ — it is 0 − (2a³/3 − a²/2 + 3a) and 2a³/3 → −∞ as a → −∞ — but stresses that even if the two halves had run to +∞ and −∞, cancelling them would not be permitted.

questions.q: Work Type II Example 1 in full: determine whether ∫₋₁² dx/x⁴ converges or diverges. Justify the split, evaluate each piece with correct signs, and say what the naive Fundamental Theorem answer would have been and why it is visibly impossible.
questions.concept: The interior-discontinuity split, done with the signs right
questions.why: A good answer notices first that 1/x⁴ is undefined at x = 0 and that 0 lies strictly inside [−1, 2], so slide 8 clause 3 applies: ∫₋₁² = ∫₋₁⁰ + ∫₀², i.e. lim(c→0⁻)∫₋₁ᶜ dx/x⁴ + lim(b→0⁺)∫_b² dx/x⁴. The antiderivative is ∫x⁻⁴dx = x⁻³/(−3) = −1/(3x³). Left piece: (−1/(3c³)) − (−1/(3(−1)³)) = −1/(3c³) − 1/3, and as c → 0⁻ the number c³ is small and NEGATIVE, so −1/(3c³) → +∞; the piece tends to +∞. Right piece: (−1/24) − (−1/(3b³)) = −1/24 + 1/(3b³) → +∞ as b → 0⁺. Neither limit is finite, so the integral diverges. The naive route gives [−1/(3x³)]|₋₁² = −1/24 − 1/3 = −3/8, which is impossible because 1/x⁴ is strictly positive wherever it is defined, so no correct answer can be negative — that impossibility is the diagnostic. A strong answer also notes that the slide's own line, '→ −∞ as c → 0⁻', has the sign wrong; both pieces go to +∞.

questions.q: Decide each of these by the lecturer's comparison template, showing every inequality step and naming f, g and the clause used: (a) ∫₂^∞ cos²(x)/x^(3/2) dx, and (b) ∫₃^∞ dx/√(x⁴ + 9).
questions.concept: Running the comparison template on a bounded numerator and on a root
questions.why: For (a): since 0 ≤ cos²(x) ≤ 1 for every x, and x^(3/2) > 0 on [2, ∞), dividing the inequality by the positive x^(3/2) preserves it, giving 0 ≤ cos²(x)/x^(3/2) ≤ 1/x^(3/2). Set f(x) = 1/x^(3/2) and g(x) = cos²(x)/x^(3/2), so 0 ≤ g ≤ f. By Note 1, p = 3/2 > 1, so ∫₂^∞ dx/x^(3/2) converges; by clause 1, ∫₂^∞ cos²(x)/x^(3/2) dx converges. No value is obtained. For (b): for x ≥ 3, x⁴ + 9 ≥ x⁴, so √(x⁴ + 9) ≥ √(x⁴) = x² (valid because x > 0), and taking reciprocals of positive quantities REVERSES the inequality: 1/√(x⁴ + 9) ≤ 1/x². Set f(x) = 1/x² and g(x) = 1/√(x⁴ + 9), so 0 ≤ g ≤ f. By Note 1, p = 2 > 1, so ∫₃^∞ dx/x² converges; by clause 1, ∫₃^∞ dx/√(x⁴ + 9) converges. Credit in both parts for stating the non-negativity, for the reciprocal flip in (b), and for saying explicitly that the conclusion is convergence and not a value; a strong answer notes that squaring the cosine in (a) is what makes 0 ≤ g hold, and that with cos x alone the theorem's hypothesis would fail.

checks.topic: Numerical Lorentz-force work: computing q*v*B*sin(theta) and qE and combining them as vectors rather than as numbers, showing the magnetic force does zero work, evaluating the orbit radius r = mv/(qB) and period T = 2*pi*m/(qB) and the helical pitch, applying F = B*I*L*sin(theta) with the length converted to metres and the angle taken from the current, finding the selector speed v = E/B, converting gauss to tesla, and getting wavelength and photon energy from c = f*lambda and E = h*f, with the unit, angle, sign and direction traps at each step

questions.q: A charge q = +4.0 microcoulomb moves at v = 2.5x10^5 m/s, its velocity making 30 degrees with a uniform magnetic field B = 0.60 T, and a uniform electric field of magnitude E = 1.2x10^3 V/m is present in the same region. The magnitude of the magnetic force on the charge is:
questions.concept: F = q*v*B*sin(theta), theta between v and B
questions.why: q*v = (4.0x10^-6)(2.5x10^5) = 1.0; times B = 0.60; times sin(30 degrees) = 0.500 gives 0.30 N. (a) 0.60 N ignores the angle, the value that applies only when v is perpendicular to B. (c) 0.52 N is q*v*B*cos(30 degrees), the sin/cos swap. (d) 1.0 N is q*v with B dropped entirely, and its units are not newtons.

questions.q: For the same charge and fields, the magnitude of the electric force is:
options: zero, since the electric force acts only on charges at rest
questions.concept: F_E = qE, with no angle and no velocity in it
questions.why: (4.0x10^-6)(1.2x10^3) = 4.8x10^-3 N, directed along E because q is positive. (a) applies the same sin(30 degrees) to the electric term; the angle belongs to the cross product only and qE has no angular factor. (b) multiplies qE by v, importing the velocity from the magnetic formula and destroying the units. (d) inverts the correct condition: it is the magnetic force that vanishes for a charge at rest, while qE acts whether the charge moves or not.

questions.q: For the same charge, the work done by the magnetic force while it travels 5.0 cm along its path is:
questions.concept: The magnetic force is perpendicular to v, so it does no work over any distance
questions.why: The integral of F.dl with dl along v and F perpendicular to v is exactly zero, over 5.0 cm or over 5.0 km; the charge leaves the region with the speed and kinetic energy it entered with. (a) is (0.30)(0.050), force times distance with no check on the angle between them. (b) inserts a cos(30 degrees), which is the angle between v and B and has nothing to do with the angle between F and dl - that angle is 90 degrees and its cosine is zero. (c) is the work done by the electric force, the right calculation applied to the wrong force.

questions.q: A proton enters a uniform field B = 0.25 T at v = 3.0x10^6 m/s, moving perpendicular to the field. The radius of its circular path is:
questions.concept: r = m*v/(q*B)
questions.why: q*B = (1.60x10^-19)(0.25) = 4.00x10^-20 and m*v = (1.67x10^-27)(3.0x10^6) = 5.01x10^-21, so r = 0.125 m, about 0.13 m. (b) 7.98 m is the expression inverted, q*B/(m*v), a reciprocal length whose units alone condemn it. (c) 6.8x10^-5 m uses the electron mass for a proton, an error of a factor 1836 that still looks like a radius. (d) 0.063 m is exactly half, from confusing radius with half the diameter or importing a spurious factor of one half.

questions.q: That proton's speed is now doubled, everything else unchanged. Its radius and period become:
options: radius 0.25 m, period unchanged at 2.6x10^-7 s
radius 0.25 m, period doubled to 5.2x10^-7 s
radius unchanged at 0.13 m, period halved to 1.3x10^-7 s
radius 0.063 m, period halved to 1.3x10^-7 s
questions.concept: r is proportional to v, but T = 2*pi*m/(q*B) contains no v
questions.why: Doubling the speed doubles the radius to 0.25 m while the period stays at 2*pi*(1.67x10^-27)/(4.00x10^-20) = 2.6x10^-7 s: a circle twice as large covered at twice the speed takes exactly as long. (b) gets the radius right then assumes a bigger circle must take longer, forgetting that the speed rose too. (c) fixes the radius and shortens the period, the picture of a particle confined to a fixed track going round faster. (d) shrinks the radius, inverting the dependence on v altogether.

questions.q: A straight wire of length 40 cm carries 5.0 A and lies at 60 degrees to a uniform field of 0.20 T. The force on the wire is:
questions.concept: F = B*I*L*sin(theta), theta from the current to B, with L in metres
questions.why: L = 0.40 m, B*I*L = (0.20)(5.0)(0.40) = 0.40, times sin(60 degrees) = 0.866 gives 0.35 N. (a) 0.40 N ignores the angle and is the maximum, reached only at 90 degrees. (b) 0.20 N is B*I*L*cos(60 degrees), the sin/cos swap, made plausible by the tidy factor of one half. (c) 35 N leaves L as 40 cm, a factor of 100; a 35 N force on a thin wire would be visible across the room.

questions.q: A beam passes undeflected through crossed fields E = 4.8x10^4 V/m and B = 0.12 T. The selected speed is:
options: 4.0x10^5 m/s for a proton but 2.0x10^5 m/s for an electron of half the momentum
questions.concept: v = E/B, containing neither q nor m
questions.why: v = (4.8x10^4)/(0.12) = 4.0x10^5 m/s. (a) is E times B, multiplying where the balance qE = q*v*B requires dividing. (c) is B/E, the ratio inverted, and 2.5 micrometres per second is not a beam speed. (d) is the misconception the selector exists to defeat: q cancels from both sides and m never enters, so every species that passes does so at the same speed, and momentum is irrelevant to the balance - mass and charge matter only in the second, magnet-only stage where r = m*v/(q*B).

questions.q: A magnet is specified as producing 3.5x10^4 gauss. In SI units this is:
questions.concept: 1 T = 10^4 G, so divide by 10^4
